chapter_theme: Songs at Palani (பழநி), second part: the poet confesses infatuation with women and courtesans who swear lasting love and take a man's wealth, the bonds of kin and body, neglected worship and the coming of Death, and asks for Murugan's feet; the praise names Murugan as the child born of Siva's grace, as Siva's teacher, and, in 126, as the boy Uruttiracanman who judged the Tamil of the Sangam poets.
structure_note: Most songs keep the two halves. 127 is praise alone. 122, 123, 124 and 129 confess something other than women: the bonds of kin and body (122), worship never done (123), the sects and the round of births (124), and the hour of death (129). 126 and 130 are built on catalogues of comparisons for a woman's eyes and body.

119.reading: The poet describes women who smear themselves with sandal paste and musk, chew betel and in lovemaking pass it from their mouths into their lovers', women of many minds, and asks Murugan to tell him on what day he will let go of his attachment to them. The praise names him lord of the hunter girl of the millet field, whose breasts he embraced, the one who delighted in the vel that ended the murderous asura clans, and the guru who dwells always at Palani.
119.nuance: பலபல சிந்தை மாதர்கள், women of many minds, is the charge of divided hearts. The word கசனை, which carries the plea, I take as attachment from context; I cannot confirm the word.

120.reading: The poet, caught by infatuation with women's sleepless eyes, their humming-bee hair, budding breasts and Kama's sugarcane bow, says his body burns in the moonlight and his life loosens in pain, and asks whether he must die with the thought of these women living in his heart. The praise names the vel wet with flesh and hung with bells and fresh flowers, the chest whose garland was crushed by the hunter girl's breasts, and Guha on the many-coloured peacock, at Palani hill.
120.nuance: அவர் குடிபுகுந்த நினைவொடும் இறந்துபடலாமோ: the fear is not death itself but dying with the women settled (குடிபுகுந்த) in the heart, where the Lord should be. The love-sickness uses the stock moonlight and Kama's bow (மதவேள்) of Tamil love poetry.

121.reading: The poet describes courtesans (விலைமாதர்) who swear that until life leaves the body they will never once slacken in their union with a man, then turn against those they joined before, strip them of their wealth, go out to meet the next ones and talk sweetly to them night and day; he asks Murugan to come on the peacock and free him from their net. The praise names Hari who danced with the cowherd women when mocked as a curd thief, the Lord of Kazhi, Marudur, Maraikkadu, Marugal and Dhanushkodi whose gift Murugan is, and Palani where carp leap up to fight the stars.
121.nuance: The song turns on the false oath (சூள்): உயிர்க்கூடு விடுமளவும், until the body's nest is left, is the promise; திரவியம் அதுடைத்து, wiping out his wealth, is the outcome. The shrine list names Siva's Tamil temples (சீகாழி, மருதூர், மறைக்காடு, மருகல், தனுக்கோடி) as one Lord's.

122.reading: A short song: the poet names the bonds of the world, pasu and pasam, kin, mother, father, home and children, and the agitation of the body's filth and breath, and asks for grace so that his mind's balance is not destroyed by them. The praise names Murugan as the son adorned with Ganga, arugu grass, poolai and thumbai flowers, Saravanabhava, nephew of Mukunda, who studies the many arts and the Siva Agamas, at Palani.
122.nuance: உலக பசு பாச தொந்தம் uses the Saiva Siddhanta terms pasu and pasam for the ordinary ties of family. The flowers of சலம் அறுகு பூளை தும்பை are Siva's; the line can make Murugan wear them or make him the son (சேய்) of the one who does. பலகலை சிவாகமங்கள் பயில்வோன் makes Murugan a student or master of the Agamas.

123.reading: A short song: the poet confesses that he has never once known the god with love for his two feet, never worshipped at Palani, never set his aim on the rare life, and asks whether he will not give up the burden of desire and think of ending birth. The praise calls Murugan, in four rhyming lines, the plunderer of the demons' city, the guardian of devotees who worship him, the one who delights in giving and in honoured verse, and the bodyguard (வேளைக்காரன்) of the hunters' little girl.
123.nuance: The four epithets end in காரப் பெருமாளே, and the last makes the Lord a servant: வேளைக்காரன் was a king's sworn bodyguard, here in Valli's service. ஆசைப் பாடை may be the burden or suffering (பாடு) of desire, or desire as a bier; the split is uncertain.

124.reading: The poet describes sectarians who cannot recognise one another's truth, men of the senses on no single path, who think the body permanent, steal, lie and kill, fall into Death's hell and are born again to swim the sea of the two deeds; he asks Murugan to give him holy ash and his feet, so that he may gain the supreme knowledge and the path to Siva. The praise names the guru of true knowledge who burned the three cities and Kama with a smile and an eye, the Lord whose dance Saraswati and Maheswari praise, and Murugan's vel of true knowledge that powdered crores of asuras when Indra, Brahma and Vishnu cried out, at ancient Palani where the Vedas hail him as the hunter girl's husband.
124.nuance: மதவிசாரர், the sect-disputers, open the song, and the remedy is not a better doctrine but a sign and a gift: நீறு வடிவுற அருளி, grant the ash to take form on me. The vel is called மெய்ஞ்ஞான அயில், the lance of true knowledge. The line மறைவரின் அனைய கோலம் is unclear to me.

125.reading: The poet describes women whose maids run back and forth to call men and coax them, women who dress their hair, tuck in betel rolls and smear agil and civet on their breasts before embracing with a show of love, and asks whether a bond with such hussies is fitting. The praise names Palani in Vaikavur country, where bees drink from lotus pools in the fields and sing and the conches spill pearls, and Murugan who embraced the faultless hunter girl.
125.nuance: சேடிமார்கள் பசப்ப, maids who coax, is the household of a courtesan, but the song does not name money. சிறுக்கிகள் உறவாமோ, is a bond with such hussies fit, makes the confession a question of the company he keeps.

126.reading: The poet describes women's eyes as having defeated every standard of comparison, imprisoning the sea, branding the bee, leaving poison fit only for the beggar-god's food, sending the carp into the pond and the deer into the forest, putting the mango slice in salt, the spear in the fire, trampling Yama and breaking the sword, and asks whether he will fall to the eye-corners of these wily women. The praise names Murugan as the one born, by Siva's command, in a merchant family under the name Rudrajanma, who taught Sanaka, Agastya, Pulastya and Sanatkumara, and made the forty-nine poets of the plank understand without fault the sense of the three Tamils, grammar and literature; he is the true guru, at Palani.
126.nuance: The first half is a single conceit: each thing a poet compares eyes to has been beaten and put away. The second names the story of the dumb child Uruttiracanman (ருத்ரஜன்மப் பெயர்), born to a merchant (செட்டி), who judged the commentaries of the Sangam's poets (சதுபத்துநவப் புலவர், the forty-nine on the plank, பலகை). Murugan is thus the judge of Tamil itself. Several lines of the first half are compressed, and my split of them is not certain.

127.reading: A song of praise only: Murugan is the brother of the pot-bellied, small-eyed elephant-faced god who eats gram, puffed rice, beans, fruit and sugarcane; the hero whose emerald peacock circled the northern mountain in an instant, shaking its peak; the bridegroom of Indra's daughter and the hunter girl; and the lisping child given by the grace of Pasupati, who wears the moon, konrai and the river, who came to Palani.
127.nuance: The song is a family portrait: the brother, the two wives, the father. The peacock circling the mountain in a moment may allude to the race round the world for the fruit that tradition ties to Palani, but the text names no fruit. மழலை மொழி மதலை, the lisping child, is Murugan as an infant.

128.reading: The poet says that though his mind is anxious and infatuated with the jewelled breasts of women who block the way to release, he will not forget Murugan's golden body, six faces, twelve mighty arms, the victorious vel, the peacock that holds the snake, the cock whose cry shakes the seven worlds, and the new lotus feet in which devotees thrive. The praise names Raghava, who gladly gave the long crown to the younger brother when the elder of the sun's line fell fighting, as Murugan's uncle, and Palani where the eleven Rudras keep the lamps and flowers fall from the kalpaka forest.
128.nuance: The song is a vow, not a plea: மறவேனே, I will not forget, answers ஆகிலும், even though, so the remembered form is set against the infatuation. கதியை விலக்கும் மாதர்கள், women who turn one from release, names what is at stake. The brother given the crown is Sugriva, son of the Sun, by the details.

129.reading: The poet asks that the cruel trident-bearer who drives the great black buffalo, rushing in with his tightening noose when lives end, and the jackals and fire that claim the body, not come near him, and that Murugan give him his feet, which shine with closeness, knowledge and kinship. The praise names him the son born of the grace of the Lord joined to the mountain's daughter, dwelling at old Palani where the ploughmen's shares write in the fields, the one who pierced the hard mountain with the vel so that even Mayan feared, and the Lord with lance, peacock, valour, colour and beauty.
129.nuance: Death here is திரிசூலன், the trident-bearer, with buffalo and noose; the jackal and fire (நரியும் எரியும் உரிமை) are the claims on the corpse, earth burial or burning. செறிவும் அறிவும் உறவும் lists what the feet give; the meaning of each word there is not certain.

130.reading: The poet asks a run of questions about women: is the hair a black cloud or darkness, the face the full moon, the eyes arrows or a vel, the breasts golden Meru or pots, the belly the banyan leaf on which Vishnu sleeps, the waist a thread; seeking such women like golden peacocks, he calls himself worthless and asks that after his hundred years pass his life may come to Murugan's two lotus feet. The praise names him son of Mahesvara who burned the three cities and Kama with his eye, the vel that freed the gods from Sura's prison, nephew of Narayana, and son of the merciful goddess, at Palani praised by the fourteen worlds.
130.nuance: The comparisons are put as questions (மேகமதோ இருளோ), the infatuated man's own way of seeing. கசடன், the worthless one, is the self-judgement. வயதாய் ஒரு நூறு செல்வதனின் மேல் I read as asking for the feet when the full life is over; it could also mean before.

131.reading: The poet describes courtesans who sway their breasts, talk of money with carp-eyed glances, tug at clothes, laugh, cause infatuation and confusion and then embrace, women who snatch a man's wealth; he asks that, without falling into their ways in this Kali age, Murugan fix him in devotion to Siva's state. The praise names him son of the god who burned the three cities with a small smile, the vel that made the sea cry out and the thieves flee, and the bridegroom of the hunter girl at Palani, where monkeys tear open fragrant fruit and play.
131.nuance: கயல்விழிப் பார்வையில் பொருள் பேசி, talking of money with the eyes, and பொருட்பறி மாதர், women who snatch wealth, name the trade. The plea places the poet in the Kali age (இக்கலியுகத்தே) and asks for சிவபதம், Siva's state, from Murugan. The split of சிவபதபத்தே is uncertain.

132.reading: The poet says that, praising women's dark, wide eyes as carp and swallowing the poison of the waist where the garment gathers, he has passed many days in a body of fierce deeds driven by passion, and asks that he not falter on the way fate set but gain Murugan's high feet fragrant with garlands. The praise names Muruga of the kadamba with the hunter girl at his side, whose vel defeated the deceitful asura who came with the old sea when the gods cried for justice, and who settled at Palani after seeing the shaven-headed Jains on rows of stakes.
132.nuance: விதிவழி நின்று, standing on fate's path, sets the confession inside fate and deed (வினை உடல், the body of deeds). பறிதலைக் குண்டர் கழுநிரை கண்டு, having seen the hair-plucked Jains in rows on stakes, is again the Madurai story told of Sambandar, now given to Murugan.

133.reading: The poet asks not to be bewildered by the infatuation that women stir with sidelong eyes like the arrows Kama shoots from his sugarcane bow and with breasts that rival a rutting elephant, and asks whether he, a servant who praises Murugan, will have the day when Murugan, by grace, teaches him the meaning of the Veda, as he did when Rudra came near asking for grace. The praise names the Lord on the great peacock that shook mountains, giant demons and the seven seas, with twelve jewelled arms like hills, lord of Vayalur, the guru who defeats poverty and enmity for those who recite and read the Thiruppugazh, at Palani where hunters' smoke rises among the clouds.
133.nuance: உருத்திரனும் விருத்திபெற ... மறை அடுத்து பொருள் உணர்த்து நாள்: the poet asks for the teaching Murugan gave Siva, and asks it as அடிமை, a servant. The song names its own book: திருப்புகழை உரைப்பவர்கள் படிப்பவர்கள் are promised victory over want (மிடி) and enmity. The syntax of the Rudra line is not certain.

links.note: Both turn on a courtesan's vow never to part: the Naladiyar woman who promised to be like the gem on its thread turns like a ram's horn, and 121's women who swear union until death strip the man and go to meet the next. The Naladiyar asks the heart to leave; 121 asks Murugan to come.

The Kural cannot decide whether the girl's look is Death, an eye or a doe; 126 claims the eyes have beaten the deer into the forest and trampled Yama himself. The same comparisons, but the Kural's lover wonders and the poet of 126 fears to fall.

Both set Murugan against Death's buffalo and noose at the hour of death; 8 asks him to come on the peacock, 129 asks that Death not come near at all and adds the jackals and fire that claim the corpse.
Both are confessions of worship never done, built as a list of negatives (தொழுதிலன், சேவித்தறியேனே); 8 ends at the hour of death, 123 at the wish to end birth.
Both give Murugan the impaling of the Jains, the Madurai story told of Sambandar: 17 names the Tamil mouth that set them on stakes, 132 has him settle at Palani after seeing them there.
12 praises Murugan for giving the knowledge to Siva; 133 asks whether the poet, as a servant, will receive the same teaching of the Veda's meaning.

source_issues: Song 126: one corrupt character in பவனு஡ணாக் (line 3); probably பவனூணாக், the beggar's food.
Song 133: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 18); clearly வயலூரா.
